article.headline: Massive Adopts llms.txt to Reduce AI Hallucinations in Stock Apps
article.lede: Massive, Inc., a financial data API provider, has added llms.txt support to its developer documentation — a move designed to give AI coding assistants direct, structured access to its API specs. The idea is simple: when an LLM can read clean markdown instead of scraping HTML, it is less likely to invent method names, parameters, or endpoints that don't exist. The announcement reflects a broader push, still in early stages, to make the web more legible to machines.
article.body:
**llms.txt** is a proposed convention — modelled loosely on the decades-old `robots.txt` standard that tells search-engine crawlers where to go — that asks websites to publish a clean, markdown-formatted summary of their content at a predictable path. Where `robots.txt` was written for Googlebot, `llms.txt` is written for language models: no navigation chrome, no JavaScript payloads, no cookie banners, just the information a developer or AI assistant actually needs.

For an API provider like Massive the stakes are concrete. A developer using an AI coding assistant to integrate a stock-data feed is only as good as the LLM's knowledge of that API. If the model's training data is stale, incomplete, or garbled from a noisy web scrape, it will generate plausible-looking but wrong function calls — a common failure mode when building against fast-moving or niche APIs. By hosting a canonical `llms.txt`, Massive is effectively saying: here is the authoritative spec; please read this, not whatever you absorbed during pre-training.

Alongside the llms.txt rollout, Massive has also shipped an "open as markdown" feature that lets developers send a specific section of the docs — the exact endpoint or data schema they need — directly into a prompt. That is a small but useful ergonomic improvement: instead of copy-pasting from a browser tab, the relevant spec travels with the question.

One claim in the announcement deserves scrutiny. The promise of "zero LLM hallucinations" is marketing, not engineering. *llms.txt* improves the accuracy of documentation-grounded tasks; it does not eliminate hallucinations, which can arise from reasoning errors, ambiguous prompts, or anything outside the scope of the provided text. The standard is a useful signal-to-noise improvement, not a correctness guarantee.

concepts.definition: A proposed web convention where a site publishes a clean, markdown-formatted file at `/llms.txt` (analogous to `robots.txt`) so that AI assistants can read accurate, structured content without scraping HTML. The goal is to give language models a reliable, up-to-date description of a service or API, reducing the chance that they rely on stale or garbled training data.

When a large language model generates confident-sounding text that is factually wrong or fabricated — for example, inventing an API method that does not exist. Hallucinations are more common when the model's training data is sparse, outdated, or inconsistent with the current state of a system.

A plain-text file that websites have placed at their root since the 1990s to instruct web crawlers which pages to index or ignore. It is the historical template that llms.txt consciously echoes, applying the same 'machine-readable convention at a known path' idea to AI assistants rather than search engines.

article.fact_check: The tweet's claim of "zero LLM hallucinations" is an overstatement. Providing structured documentation via llms.txt reduces hallucinations that stem from incomplete or stale API knowledge, but it cannot prevent hallucinations that arise from reasoning errors, ambiguous instructions, or topics outside the supplied text. No documentation format can guarantee zero hallucinations from a language model.
